title: Stew Pletcher as a jazz trumpeter
summary: Sauter corrects an earlier interview remark and says he learned most about jazz from Pletcher's reaching and recouping.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Stu was wonderful. In an interview once we were talking about Stu, they asked me about him, I said Stu was never very good, but that is not the case. He was not an accomplished trumpet player, but as a jazz musician he was superb, and I didn't make that clear, and I would like to make that clear now.
I know if he ever heard that interview it must have hurt him. It was not done maliciously.
Michael Brooks talked to you when they did the Red Norvo reissue, at Columbia Special Products; right?
I got the impression from what you said that he just wasn't a very good--an extremely polished musician, but he was a talented jazz trumpet player.
If you got that, that was fine, because I learned--I think I learned more jazz from Stuie because he would always try for things and miss, but it was his recouping that made the thing--
Miles Davis has made a career out of that.
That's right, and so have I.
To me most of the fun is reaching for something, not quite knowing where you're going and if you miss, use it, and I learned that from Stu and I think that's an artistic precept.
No, I didn't get that impression at all.
